Question: A box contains exactly five chips, three red and two white. Chips are randomly removed one at a time without replacement until all the red chips are drawn or all the white chips are drawn. What is the probability that the last chip drawn is white?
Solution:
Method 1: Imagine completing all five draws

Imagine arranging all five chips in a random draw order before applying the stopping rule. This produces the same actual draws up to the stopping time, while letting us examine the final position.

The process stops when one color makes its final appearance. If the fifth chip in the complete order is red, both whites appear before the final red, so the process stops on the second white. If the fifth chip is white, all three reds appear before the second white, so the process stops on the third red. These two cases cover every possible order.

Thus the last chip actually drawn is white exactly when the fifth chip in the complete order is red. Each individual chip is equally likely to occupy that position, and three of the five chips are red. Therefore the probability is \(\boxed{3/5}\), choice \(\boxed{D}\).

Method 2: List the possible white-ending sequences

For the last draw to be white, the second white must appear while at least one red remains. Consequently, it can appear only on draw \(2\), \(3\), or \(4\).

Write \(R\) for red and \(W\) for white. The possible stopped sequences are
\[
WW;\qquad RWW,\ WRW;\qquad RRWW,\ RWRW,\ WRRW.
\]
This list is exhaustive: before the final white there must be exactly one white and either zero, one, or two reds. Every listed sequence avoids exhausting either color earlier.

The length-two sequence has probability
\[
\frac25\cdot\frac14=\frac1{10}.
\]
Each length-three sequence has probability
\[
\frac{3\cdot2\cdot1}{5\cdot4\cdot3}=\frac1{10},
\]
and each length-four sequence has probability
\[
\frac{3\cdot2\cdot2\cdot1}{5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2}=\frac1{10}.
\]
In these products, the numerators count the available chips of the required colors. Their order changes between sequences, but their product does not. The denominators decrease because chips are not replaced.

The six stopped sequences are mutually exclusive, so their probabilities add to
\[
6\left(\frac1{10}\right)=\boxed{\frac35}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{D}\).
